_meta.source: JRC ASAP (Anomaly hot Spots of Agricultural Production)
_meta.notes: Current-season agricultural stress from the EC Joint Research Centre's ASAP monthly expert assessment. Latest assessment per country from the full 2016-present series; most recent date in this run 2026-10-11. hotspot_code: 0 no hotspot, 1 hotspot, 2 major hotspot. ASAP's raw hs_code 3 means NOT ASSESSED, not a severity above 2 — those countries (8 in this run) carry hotspot_code null and stress_score null. NULL IS NOT ZERO: no assessment is not an all-clear, and several unassessed countries have dozens of subnational crop warnings standing (units_crop_warning is populated regardless of code). stress_score 0-100 is banded by the JRC verdict (0-20 / 40-70 / 75-100 for codes 0/1/2) and spread within band by units_crop_warning normalised against that country's own historical maximum — so the expert verdict always dominates the ranking and the count only breaks ties. COVERAGE IS NOT GLOBAL: ASAP monitors 79 food-insecure countries only. A country absent from this payload is one ASAP does not watch (USA, Ukraine, Brazil, India, Australia among them) — absence must NOT be presented as an absence of stress. Unlike Aqueduct baseline and CCKP normals, this is a current-season signal and goes stale monthly; ASAP publishes around the 10th.

AFG.comment:
In Afghanistan, harvest of spring wheat and summer crops finalized or will finalize in November for irrigated rice with good prospects thanks to average to above average crop biomass. Planting of winter wheat and barley has started in October under favourable rainfall conditions. These good rainfall conditions are forecast to continue through March according to the Copernicus C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.
 Afghanistan continues to face high levels of hunger with about 15.9 million people (out of about 45 million people) estimated in acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 or above) for the period September-October 2026, as a result of prolonged economic deterioration, recurrent drought, refugee returns, declining humanitarian aid and decreasing remittances according to the latest [https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Afghanistan_AFI_AMN_Sep2026_Sep2027_Snapshot.pdf] IPC report from 13 October 2026 .

AGO.comment: Land preparation and the planting of cereal crops, primarily maize, have begun in parts of Angola. However, a slight delay in the start of the season has been observed across central regions. According to [https://fews.net/southern-africa/angola/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), this delay is likely driven by a forecast El Niño-induced late onset of the rainy season alongside severe national fertilizer shortages, which have prompted even better-off farmers to delay and scale back land preparation. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 points to a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions, particularly across central and southern areas. Conversely, only the interior northeastern provinces are projected to receive near-average to slightly above-average precipitation. As reported by [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=AGO] FAO GIEWS (03/09), this dry outlook is heavily influenced by the ongoing El Niño event that emerged in June, which is historically associated with suppressed rainfall totals across much of Southern Africa. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

BDI.comment: Planting of Season A crops, including beans, maize and sorghum, is underway. Rainfall has been average over the past three dekads, but biomass remains below average across the country, with 71% of cropland in Cankuzo, 75% in Muyinga and 74% in Ruyigi showing poor vegetation conditions. Linked to the ongoing El Niño, [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Copernicus seasonal forecasts point to wetter-than-usual conditions in the coming months. According to [https://fews.net/east-africa/burundi/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET, the Northern Lowlands are expected to deteriorate to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) during the October–January lean season following consecutive below-average harvests in 2026, while fuel shortages, the closed border with Rwanda and staple prices 10–50% above the five-year average continue to constrain food access. Season A production is also expected to be below average due to fertilizer shortages and the delayed onset of rains, and strong El Niño-related rainfall is likely to cause flooding, landslides and localized crop losses.

BEN.comment: The first-season maize harvest and the harvest of rainfed rice were completed in the southern parts of the country in September. Overall prospects remain average, sustained by generally favourable, near-average cumulative rainfall during crop development. Planting of second-season maize was completed in September, and crop conditions in the central and southern bimodal areas are average to above-average as of mid-October. In the North, which experiences only one rainy season, the harvesting of cereals began in October and is expected to be completed by the end of November. However, localized agricultural challenges persist; particularly poor crop and rangeland biomass conditions are observed in Borgou province, where nearly 45% of the active crop area and approximately 40% of the active rangeland area are affected by a greenness anomaly. The provinces of Alibori and Atakora are similarly impacted, though to a lesser extent, with around 30% of their active crop areas exhibiting vegetation stress. These environmental stressors compound ongoing humanitarian challenges; according to the [https://reliefweb.int/report/benin/wfp-benin-country-brief-october-2026] WFP (Benin Country Brief, October 2026), "the insecurity risks and ongoing displacement in the northern and central regions of the country limit vulnerable populations' access to basic services and disrupt education, livelihoods, and community protection systems.".

BFA.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 maize, sorghum, and millet is underway across the country and is expected to conclude in December. Driven by a highly irregular rainfall distribution, the agricultural season is suffering from widespread moisture stress that severely impacts 50% to 70% of the active crop area in the central regions (specifically Centre-Ouest, Plateau-Central, and Centre). Similarly, rangeland biomass conditions in these same central areas are below-average, with approximately 35% to 60% of the active rangeland affected by a greenness anomaly. Conversely, good rains between mid-September and early October have improved vegetation in regions previously hindered by poor crop development, such as the Centre-Nord, Nord, Boucle du Mouhoun, Hauts-Bassins, Centre-Est, and Sud-Ouest. Despite these late-season recoveries, deficits remain; according to [https://fews.net/west-africa/burkina-faso/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), due to a late seasonal onset, prolonged August-to-September dry spells, and recent grain-eating bird infestations, agropastoral production in Burkina Faso is projected to fall below last season's levels, with severe yield drops for maize and poorly replenished pastures in the north.

BGD.comment: In Bangladesh, prospects are very favourable for Aman rice (35% of the country total rice production) to be harvested in November-December as crop biomass is well above average across all divisions despite very low rainfall in the last month (20 to 25% of the average rainfall of 20 Sept - 20 Oct).

BOL.comment: In October, rice cycle should be in the sowing stage, mostly in the provinces of Santa Cruz and Beni. Prospects are not favourable as during October, rice sowing faced severe delays and area reductions driven by a dual crisis of fuel/diesel shortages and drought in several regions. On October 31st, Bolivia has declared a nationwide state of emergency for drought and adverse climate events to free up resources to deal with the effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon ([http://www.gacetaoficialdebolivia.gob.bo/normas/descargarNrms/405022] Gov.bo). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" style="] Copernicus C3S Multimodel, the most likely scenario is lower than normal rainfall persisting through the end of the year, especially for the southern western part of the country where the probability is very high.

BWA.comment: Planting of summer cereal crops in the main western and southern producing provinces is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions nationwide. Furthermore, the JRC ASAP forecast warnings for both [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/ebb9f57d] crops and [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6ca9147] rangelands point to a high probability of dry conditions across agropastoral areas for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

CAF.comment: Rice and cassava are in their development stage, with harvests expected to start in late November. Rainfall has been average nationwide over the past 30 days, although pockets of below-average biomass persist in Fertit and Yade, where 30% and 9% of active cropland, respectively, shows poor vegetation conditions. The ongoing El Niño is expected to bring [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] wetter-than-usual conditions across the country in the coming months. According to [https://fews.net/west-africa/central-african-republic/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET, insecurity and isolation will sustain Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes through January 2027 in Haut-Mbomou, Haute-Kotto, Vakaga and parts of the northwest, while more stable central and southern areas remain in Stressed (IPC Phase 2) as ongoing harvests benefit from generally favorable rainfall. Meanwhile, cereal prices remain high in isolated areas, with maize in Birao costing about twice as much as in Bangui, and fuel shortages are expected to keep transport costs and import prices elevated.

CMR.comment: The harvest of main maize crops in the central and southern parts of the country was completed in September, while the planting of second-season maize crops concluded in October. In northern unimodal areas (specifically the North and Far North regions) where sorghum and millet are predominantly grown, harvesting is currently underway. Crop conditions are generally favourable thanks to average rainfall received since the start of the cropping season. Furthermore, rangeland conditions across the country were average to slightly above-average as of mid-October and are expected to adequately support livestock production. However, this localized positive outlook contrasts with regional crises; according to [https://fews.net/west-africa/cameroon/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWSNET (September 2026), persistent conflict, severe rainfall deficits, and high food prices are driving widespread food insecurity across Cameroon, pushing the Far North, Northwest, and Southwest regions into Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes through January 2027, with the most vulnerable displaced households facing Emergency (IPC Phase 4) conditions due to disrupted livelihoods and reduced humanitarian aid.

COD.comment: Maize planting for the main southern season is underway, while cassava in the north is in its growth stage. Rainfall has been average across the country over the past three dekads, though biomass remains notably below average in Kongo Central (-12%), Lualaba (-18%) and South Kivu (-22%). With the ongoing El Niño, [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] wetter-than-usual conditions are expected nationwide in the coming months, except in provinces near the Atlantic coast, where drier conditions are forecast. According to [https://fews.net/southern-africa/democratic-republic-congo/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET, intensifying conflict in eastern DRC displaced over 1.71 million people in the first half of 2026, disrupting planting and sustaining Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes despite generally favorable rainfall. Meanwhile, rising food prices are reducing poor households’ purchasing power as the lean season begins, and the Ebola outbreak is disrupting cross-border trade near Uganda.

COG.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

COL.comment: In October, the main cycle of rice should have normally concluded the harvesting stage, while minor cycles of maize and rice should be in the sowing stage. Rainfall in the past month has been below normal, mostly in the northern departments of the country. El Nino drought effects are most severely felt in areas of La Guajira and the departments of Cesar and Santander, where poor vegetation conditions are observed in most cultivated areas. It’s estimated that Colombia’s total domestic maize production dropped by 6.9% compared to previous cycle estimates, raising the needs for imports ([https://www.fas.usda.gov/data/gain-report/2026/10/Grain%20and%20Feed%20Update_Bogota_Colombia_CO2026-0027.pdf] USDA).Crisis (IPC Phase 3) level food insecurity is expected to persist in Chocó and La Guajira through January 2027 according to projections ([https://fews.net/latin-america-and-caribbean/colombia/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026/print] FEWSNET). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank" style="] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very drier than normal across the country until the end of the year.

CUB.comment: In October, the main cycles of rice and maize and the sweet potato should normally be in the harvesting stage in this month.Rainfall in the past month was normal to below normal, mostly in the western part of the country but vegetation conditions look generally favorable. However, persisting energy shortages this year has prevented the smooth development of agricultural activities, including the usage of part of the irrigation system necessary to rice production. The winter, which is typically dry in Cuba, is very likely to receive heavy rains towards December through March 2027 according to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecasts, which might hinder cash crop cultivations.

DJI.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

DZA.comment: Sowings of winter cereals have started under well below average rainfall conditions in the last month (i.e. with less than 20% of the average rainfall) in a large centre going from Tiaret to Setif, and to a lesser extent in the east with about 50% of the average amount received. This is the very beginning of the cereals sowing season but if close to average rainfall is forecast for November, dry conditions should follow in December and January according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.

ECU.comment: In October, the second cycles of maize, rice and wheat should normally be in the harvesting stage, while barley should have finished its vegetation stage. A rapidly intensifying El Niño pattern brought heavy precipitation to Ecuador's Pacific coast, lowlands, and urban centres. Most affected cantons are Esmeraldas, Los Rios, Manabi. Over the past 30 days, rainfall has been up to ten times above normal in the eastern part of the country, with media reporting 39,270 people affected nationwide by heavy rainfall and flooding ([https://www.paho.org/en/natural-hazards-monitoring/natural-hazards-monitoring-2-november-2026#:~:text=According%20to%20the%20reports%2C%20114%2C048%20families%20were,2026%20and%20are%20not%20exclusively%20weekend%20impacts.] PAHO).According to IPC projections around 2.6 million people is expected to face Crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3 or above) between August and November 2026 ([https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Ecuador_Acute_Food_Insecurity_Dic2025_Nov2026_Report_Spanish.pdf] IPC). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" style="] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast very wetter than normal conditions in the coastal areas with high probability through the end of the year. Opposite forecasts are for the central and western part of the country, where conditions are likely to be normal to drier than normal.

EGY.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

ERI.comment:
Harvesting of main season crops is under way, with poor production prospects following rainfall deficits, high temperatures and persistent vegetation stress. Late-season rainfall was insufficient to reverse earlier damage, particularly in Gash Barka, Anseba and Maekel. 
Further, poor rangeland conditions continue to constrain pasture availability.

ETH.comment: As the Meher season advances towards completion, production concerns persist following below-average rainfall and high temperatures during critical crop-development stages. Conditions remain particularly poor in Tigray and parts of the eastern and northeastern agricultural areas. Expected October–December Deyr rainfall could improve pasture and water availability in southern and southeastern pastoral areas, although heavy rainfall poses localised flood risks. Conflict in Amhara and Oromia continues to disrupt agricultural activities and market access, while high food and fuel prices constrain household purchasing power and recovery. Despite a favourable Belg season in the first part of 2026, concerns over the food security outlook situation are rapidly increasing, driven by the below average Meher season conditions and by rapidly increasing food and fuel prices during the lean season, which continue to erode household purchasing power. The described conditions are of particular concern in a politically unstable situation with regional conflicts in Tigray and other areas of the country experiencing new violence.

GHA.comment: In the southern and central bimodal areas, harvesting of the 2026 main-season maize crop concluded in September with average production prospects. Planting of the second-season maize was completed in September, and crop biomass conditions as of mid-October are average to slightly above-average, except in the Central and Greater Accra regions, which have been affected by a rainfall deficit over the past month (with cumulative rainfall approximately 65% below average). In the north, harvesting of coarse grains started in October, with expected outputs ranging from average to slightly below-average. Localized production deficits are anticipated in the minor producing region of the Upper West, where a negative greenness anomaly affects more than 30% of the active crop area as of mid-October. Conversely, pasture biomass conditions across the primary grazing zones of both the north and center remain stable, staying at near-average to slightly above-average levels.

GIN.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 paddy rice crop, the country's main cereal, alongside coarse grains like maize, millet, and sorghum, started in October. Crop and rangeland conditions as of mid-October are close to average across the country, pointing to an average harvest.

GMB.comment: Harvest of main season cereal crops is underway and expected to be concluded in November. Cumulative rainfall between mid-July and beginning of October has been average. As of mid-October, crop biomass conditions are at an average to slightly above-average level, pointing to a favourable output for the 2026 season. Moreover, good pastoral biomass conditions are expected to adequately sustain livestock production. According to [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=GMB] FAO GIEWS (22/09), the government successfully mitigated the impact of high international fertilizer prices and global supply chain disruptions by maintaining the previous year's subsidy levels for the 2026 cropping season, alongside distributing free organic fertilizer and seeds to bolster national cereal production.

GNB.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

GTM.comment: October marks the final period of the primera season, with maize, beans and rice in the harvest stage, while the postrera season should normally be initiating the vegetation stage. Rainfall in the past three months was characterized by a cumulative water deficit followed by heavy rainfall in October, which increases risks for crops such as corn, beans and vegetables in Alta Verapaz and Quiché. Vegetation conditions are poor in most of the Central Area from 46% in Quiché to 85% of the cultivated areas in Baja Verapaz. A total of 697,926 families have been reported as affected across 240 municipalities in the country’s 22 departments, with most significant impacts recorded in Chiquimula (80%), followed by Quiché (63%) and Alta Verapaz (34%) ([https://precios.maga.gob.gt/novedades/10-informe-smc---octubre---2026/] MAGA GUatemala).According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very drier than normal across the country until the end of the year.

HND.comment: In October, the main cycle of maize, beans and rice should have normally concluded the harvesting stage, while the postrera of maize, beans and sorghum should be in the vegetation stage. Below average rainfall for the past three months, in particular in the Dry Corridor areas, associated with the El Niño phenomenon led to poor crop conditions in most cropping areas. Output of 2026 Primera season maize crop, which accounts for about 70 percent of the annual production, is anticipated to be well below-average level ([https://reliefweb.int/report/honduras/giews-country-brief-honduras-07-october-2026] GIEWS). In early October, critical window for land preparation and planting of the secondary Postrera crops, the country experienced extreme rainfall in low-lying border areas like Valle ([https://humanitarianaction.info/article/global-humanitarian-overview-increase-due-honduras-drought] Humanitarian Action).The situation is further exacerbated by the increase in fuel prices, among the higher in the region with over 49% year on year change and almost 6% from last month ([https://www.globalpetrolprices.com/Honduras/gasoline_prices/] GlobalPetrolPrices). The last IPC analysis indicated that 1.9 million people were in IPC Phase 3 or above between August and November 2026, including over 104.000 people in Emergency (IPC Phase 4) ([https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1165450/?iso3=HND] IPC). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very drier than normal across the country until the end of the year, providing not favorable prospects for the entire second cycle of crops.

HTI.comment: In October, the harvest of the main rice cycle is underway, while the second cycle of maize has concluded its vegetation stage and should be ready for harvest at the end of the month. Rainfall in the past month was normal to below normal in the southern part of the country. The departments of Artibonite, Grand'Anse, and Nord-Ouest show the poorest vegetation conditions and are likely to experience the sharpest drops in agricultural production due to drier-than-normal conditions induced by El Niño ([https://www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Haiti_Acute_Food_Insecurity_Sept2026_Jun2027_Report_French.pdf] IPC).However, the primary obstacle facing the country remains widespread insecurity and displacement, directly hindering normal agricultural activities. According to the latest IPC analysis, 53% of the population in Haiti, 5,94 million people is currently facing acute food insecurity at Crisis or worse level (IPC Phase 3 or above) with 1.8 million in Emergency phase (IPC Phase 4) ([https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1165467/?iso3=HTI" style="background-color: rgb(255, 255, 255);] IPC). The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=north_america" target="_blank" style="] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, it’s more likely that conditions will be wetter than no through the end of the year and beginning of 2027.

IDN.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

IRN.comment: In Iran, sowings of winter wheat and barley are underway under favourable rainfall conditions. These wetter than average conditions are expected to persist through March according to the Copernicus C3S seasonal models forecast. As for rice, most of the production has been harvested from August to September and prospects are good (8% above the 2021-2025 average according to Eqtesad-e Moaser quoted in FAO crop prospects and food situation report).

IRQ.comment: In Iraq, sowings of winter barley have started while sowings of winter wheat should take place in November and December under very favourable rainfall conditions. This good rainfall should persist through March according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. In southern Iraq, harvest of rice is underway and should conclude in November with average (Al Qadissiya) to above average (Al Najaf) prospects.

KAZ.comment: In Kazakhstan, harvest of spring wheat and barley finalized in October with favourable prospects as suggested by average to above average crop biomass (e.g. in the key oblasts of North K. R., Kostanay and Akmola). In southern Kazakhstan, sowings of winter wheat (which represents 5% of the total wheat production) are underway till November under drier than average conditions (50% below average rainfall in October in Jambyl and Almaty regions). However above average rainfall, consistent with the ongoing El Niño, is expected from November through March according to the Copernicus C3S multimodel seasonal forecast.

KEN.comment: Long-rains harvesting in unimodal areas is nearing completion, with reduced production following prolonged dry spells and rainfall deficits during critical crop-development stages. The North Rift and parts of western and central Kenya remain particularly affected. FEWS NET estimates long-rains maize production at 22–28% below the five-year average nationally, with a shortfall of approximately 43% in the North Rift. Short-rains planting is under way in most bimodal areas, although dry conditions were observed in some areas during the second dekad of October. Rainfall forecasts for the remainder of the short rains season point towards above average rains which will be critical in crop development, pasture and water availability. It is important however to bear in mind that high intensity rainfall will not be immediately beneficial to drought affected crop areas and that there is a high risk of adverse impacts including increased risk of flooding.

KGZ.comment: In Kyrgyzstan, harvest of maize and spring wheat finalized in October and prospects are good thanks to above average crop biomass. Sowings of winter cereals are underway under slightly drier than average conditions; however above average rainfall is expected from November through March according to the Copernicus C3S multimodel seasonal forecast.

KHM.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

LAO.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

LBR.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

LBY.comment: In Libya, rainfall conditions in the last month have been very favorable in the west (Tripoli area) and close to average in the east. Sowings of winter cereals normally take place from October to November but appear to be delayed around Tripoli. In the coming months, apart from November were rainfall should be close to average, drier than average moisture conditions are expected according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.

LKA.comment: In Sri Lanka, planting of main season (Maha) rice and maize is underway till end November under favourable rainfall conditions. According to the Copernicus C3S multimodel seasonal forecast, rainfall is expected above average through end December, after which drier than average conditions should prevail.

LSO.comment: Planting of summer cereal crops began in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions nationwide. Furthermore, the JRC ASAP forecast warnings for both [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/ebb9f57d] crops and [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6ca9147] rangelands point to a high probability of dry conditions across agropastoral areas for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. Despite this forecast poor start to the rainy season, reports from [https://fews.net/southern-africa/lesotho/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026) note that heavily subsidized government inputs and favourable soil moisture from recent rains are expected to support average overall planted areas. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

MAR.comment: In Morocco, sowings of winter cereals should start in November under expected close to average rainfall conditions; then rainfall is forecast to be mixed through January, namely below average in the northeast and close to average in the rest of the country according to the C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast. Similar mixed conditions occurred in the last month, with rainfall ranging from half the average rainfall for Grand Casablanca Settat to 50% above average for the regions of Fes Meknes and Beni Mellal Khenifra in the centre.

MDG.comment: In Madagascar, the 2025-2026 season has started in October with cereals and legumes planting in the Grand South (Anosy, Androy and Atsimo Andrefana) under close to average moisture conditions. In the centre and north, rice planting should start in November or December under drier than average rainfall conditions, which are expected to persist through March, according to the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast. The Grand South is estimated to have about 2 million people facing acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 and above) as a result of poor harvests due to cyclones or previous droughts (2020, 2021 and 2022) and poor socio economic conditions including rising food prices and fewer agricultural jobs according to [https://www.wfp.org/countries/madagascar] WFP.

MLI.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 coarse grains (maize, millet, and sorghum) and paddy rice crops is ongoing across the country; however, a reduced output is expected due to poor crop conditions that affected key producing regions, including Ségou, Koulikoro, Sikasso, and Mopti. As reported by [https://fews.net/west-africa/mali/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), «rainfall constraints, limited access to agricultural inputs, and reduced cultivated areas in insecure zones are negatively affecting the country's production prospects». Moreover, rangeland biomass conditions remain below average in Tombouctou, Mopti, and Ségou.

MMR.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

MOZ.comment: Land preparation and planting activities for the main cereal season are underway across Mozambique. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions nationwide. Furthermore, the JRC ASAP forecast warnings for both [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/ebb9f57d] crops and [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6ca9147] rangelands point to a high probability of dry conditions across agropastoral areas for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. This grim outlook aligns with reports from [https://fews.net/southern-africa/mozambique/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), which warn that a rapidly strengthening El Niño is expected to bring below-average, erratic rainfall to southern and central Mozambique, severely limiting agricultural activities and livestock resources, while northern areas anticipate average conditions through January 2027.

MRT.comment: The harvest of the 2026 main-season cereal crops has started in parts of the country, and crop conditions as of mid-October point to good production prospects. Similarly, rangeland biomass conditions remain at an average to slightly above-average level. However, the pastoral season faces challenges from low, unevenly distributed rainfall and ongoing cross-border transhumance restrictions with Mali; these have led to heavy livestock concentrations on scarce pastures and rising suspicions of animal disease outbreaks, despite currently satisfactory animal body conditions and higher livestock market prices ([https://reliefweb.int/report/mauritania/bulletin-de-surveillance-pastorale-de-la-mauritanie-ndeg41-aout-septembre-2026] Bulletin de Surveillance Pastorale de la Mauritanie N°41 (aout - septembre 2026)). Moreover, the country faces severe humanitarian strains from hosting over 305,000 Malian refugees, a crisis worsened by high food import dependencies and a fourfold surge in fuel prices that has driven up staple food costs in remote regions ([https://reliefweb.int/report/mauritania/wfp-mauritania-country-brief-october-2026" target="_blank] WFP Mauritania Country Brief for October 2026).

MWI.comment: Land preparation for the 2026/27 cereal cropping season has started. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions across central and southern parts of the country and average conditions in the north. This grim outlook aligns with [https://fews.net/southern-africa/malawi/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), which reports that a strengthening El Niño persisting through February 2027 is expected to drive erratic, below-average rainfall across central and southern Malawi, disrupting land preparation, crop establishment, and overall agricultural production. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

NAM.comment: Planting of summer cereal crops in main northern producing provinces is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions nationwide. Furthermore, the JRC ASAP forecast warnings for both [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/ebb9f57d] crops and [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6ca9147] rangelands point to a high probability of dry conditions across agropastoral areas for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

NER.comment: The harvest of the 2026 main season cereal crops is ongoing and it is expected to be concluded in November. Despite the poor cumulative rainfall received in the last three months, crop and rangeland conditions as of mid-October are generally average to above -average except for the region of Diffa, where crop conditions are well below-average, with more than 75% of active crop area and close to 50% of active rangeland area being affected by a greenness anomaly. According to [https://www.afriqueverte.org/index.cfm?srub=59] Afrique Verte (October 2026), despite a late start and severe 40-day dry spells that left 6% of monitored villages unplanted by late July, certain resilient varieties of millet and cowpea have successfully adapted to the extreme moisture stress across Niger's regions.

NGA.comment: Conditions for the second maize season crop, to be harvested in December across the southern bimodal areas, are average to above-average thanks to favourable cumulative rainfall received over the last month. Similarly, the harvest of rice, millet, and sorghum crops is underway in northern parts of the country under average to above-average biomass conditions. However, vegetation anomalies are observable across the Middle Belt and parts of the northeast. Particularly affected are the states of Niger and Adamawa, where approximately 40% to 50% of the active crop area exhibits a greenness anomaly. To a lesser extent, the states of Kaduna, Plateau, Nasarawa, and Kwara are also impacted, with roughly 25% to 30% of their active crop areas showing a greenness anomaly. Similarly, poor pastoral conditions are present across parts of the Middle Belt, Northeast, and Northwest, where about 30% to 45% of the active rangeland area is affected by a greenness anomaly. These localized vegetation anomalies mirror a broader national trend; according to a report from the Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS) of the US Department of Agriculture, Nigeria’s wheat, corn, and rice production for 2026–27 is projected to drop by 8%, 5%, and 6% respectively due to rising input costs, rural insecurity, and reduced farmer incentives ([https://www.world-grain.com/articles/23294-nigeria-expects-lower-wheat-rice-and-corn-production] World Grain).

NIC.comment: In October, the main cycle of sorghum concluded the harvesting stage. The postrera season of maize and beans as well as the second cycle of sorghum should normally be in the vegetation stage. Rice in the highlands should be in the harvesting stage.The postrera is highly critical for beans. Production of beans is heavily centered in Matagalpa, Jinotega, and Estelí, where the cooler highland climate and second-season rains favor bean development. Cycles in the vegetation stage have benefited from normal to above normal rainfall across the country in the last month, except in Jinotega. However, the past three months water deficit have likely depleted the necessary soil moisture for the correct development of the crops, resulting in poor vegetation conditions across all the central southern regions, ,especially in Chinandega (79%), Leon (76%) and Estelì (86%). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very direr than normal throughout the end of the year, which leave little margin of improvements for the second cycle crops development.

NPL.comment: In Nepal, rice harvest is underway with very good prospects thanks to above average crop biomass in all provinces. Wheat sowings are underway under close to average moisture conditions.

PAK.comment: In Pakistan, harvest of kharif crops (rice, maize, millet and cotton) is underway and should finalize in December. The monsoon season finalized in September and October in the south and north respectively and total rainfall in the last three months ranged from 50% below average in the south (Sindh, Balochistan) to 30% above average in the north (Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa), in agreement with the rainfall pattern associated with El Niño event. Overall, prospects are favourable thanks to average (Sindh, Balochistan) to above average (Punjab, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) crop biomass. Sowings of Rabi crops (winter wheat and barley) have started in October under close to average conditions, except in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa which received more than three time the average rainfall in the last month.

PER.comment: In October, potato and sorghum cycles should normally be in the harvesting stage, while white and yellow maize cycles should continue the sowing stage.Cumulative rainfall in the past three months has been below average in the south-eastern part of the country but with heavy rainfall events in the coastal areas. Due to the threat of El Nino induced dry spells across Andean and Amazonian regions, the emergency decree issued in August was expanded to 707 districts across 17 regions to safeguard critical agricultural water reserves ([https://www.senamhi.gob.pe/?p=avisos-detalle-hidrologicos&ca=70707&ce=4724A3F6] Gov.pe). Conversely, intense rainfall caused material damage in the districts of Matapalo, Aguas Verdes, and Zarumilla in Zarumilla Province ([https://go.ifrc.org/emergencies/8140/overview] IFRC). According to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america] Copernicus C3S Multimodel there is a higher probability of wetter than normal conditions in the coastal areas through the end of the year, while water deficit is likely to continue in the central and western part of the country.

PHL.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

PRK.comment: In DPRK, harvest of maize and rice finalized and prospects are good thanks to average to above average crop biomass across all provinces. Sowings of winter crops are underway under favourable (wetter than average) conditions.

RWA.comment: Planting of Season A crops, including beans, maize and sorghum, is nearly complete. Rainfall has been average over the past three dekads, but biomass remains below average across the country, with 69% of cropland in Iburasirazuba (Eastern Province) and 83% in Kigali showing poor vegetation conditions. Linked to the ongoing El Niño, [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Copernicus seasonal forecasts point to wetter-than-usual conditions in the coming months. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/rwanda/wfp-rwanda-country-brief-october-2026] WFP, the average cost of the food basket in Rwanda rose by 3% month-on-month and 7% year-on-year in September 2026, as food inflation and high fuel and transport costs offset the benefits of recent harvests. Refugee households have been hit particularly hard, with funding shortfalls limiting assistance to 50% of planned entitlements, while contingency planning for floods and landslides has been stepped up ahead of El Niño-driven above-average rainfall.

SDN.comment: Main-season harvesting is under way amid severe production concerns following delayed rainfall onset, prolonged moisture deficits and exceptionally high temperatures. These conditions have compounded conflict-related reductions in planted area and restricted access to fields and agricultural inputs. Poor harvests are likely to limit seasonal improvements in food availability and reduce household stocks in areas already facing extreme food insecurity. Continued displacement, destruction of agricultural assets, market disruption and restricted humanitarian access further undermine livelihoods. The May 2026 IPC analysis estimated 19.5 million people facing Crisis or worse. A subsequent partial-coverage update for June–September identified a risk of famine in 14 areas across North Darfur, South Darfur and South Kordofan under a reasonable worst-case scenario characterised by intensified conflict and further restrictions on humanitarian access and the movement of goods and people.

SEN.comment: The 2026 coarse grains (maize, millet, and sorghum) harvest is underway, while the harvesting of rice is expected to begin in November. As of mid-October, crop conditions are generally average to above-average, pointing to a favoUrable cereal harvest for 2026. Similarly, rangeland conditions remain good across the country, benefiting livestock production. However, this positive agricultural outlook has been severely disrupted by sudden extreme weather; following torrential rainfall exceeding 100 to 142 mm on October 3–4, 2026, Senegal is facing a major humanitarian and logistical crisis as widespread floods across Dakar, Kaolack, Matam, and other regions have caused fatalities, building collapses, and severe traffic paralysis, triggering an emergency response and a request for international assistance ([https://reliefweb.int/report/senegal/sen-inondation-10-2026-inondation-au-senegal-2026-10-08] Croix-Rouge Sénégalaise, IFRC, [https://reliefweb.int/map/senegal/senegal-october-floods-and-ucpm-response-dg-echo-daily-map-26102026] ECHO).

SLE.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 paddy rice, the main cereal grown in the country, and minor coarse grains (maize, millet, and sorghum), is currently underway and is expected to conclude by the end of December. As of mid-October, nationwide crop conditions are close to average, pointing to a favourable overall output for the 2026 season. The only exception is the North Western region, where more than 30% of the active crop area is affected by a greenness anomaly. Furthermore, pastoral conditions remain at an average to above-average level despite a recent nationwide rainfall deficit, with cumulative rainfall approximately 20% to 30% below average.

SLV.comment: In October, main cycle of maize should normally continue the harvesting phase, while the second cycle of maize should be concluding the sowing stage, although dry conditions observed are delaying land preparation and planting operations. The second cycle of beans should be in vegetation stage as well as the main cycle of rice and sorghum. Rainfall in the past three months was over a third below average, compromising both the primera production and the postrera cycle prospects.Due to fears of persistent El Niño drought in early 2027, farmers are shifting from maize to more resilient crops. This reduction in planted area is expected to result in below-average maize production ([https://reliefweb.int/report/el-salvador/giews-country-brief-republic-el-salvador-13-october-2026] ReliefWeb). Prospects are not favourable for the entire second cycle of crops as, according to the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=south_america" target="_blank] Copernicus C3S Multimodel forecast, there is a very high probability that conditions will be very drier than normal across the country until the end of the year.

SOM.comment: Gu 2026 crop production in Somalia was highly variable spatially. Erratic and below-average rainfall affected agricultural production in several areas, particularly in northern and central Somalia. Overall however, Gu production was better than anticipated in southern Somalia ( [https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/www.ipcinfo.org/fileadmin/user_upload/ipcinfo/docs/IPC_Somalia_Acute_Food_Insecurity_Malnutrition_Jul_Dec2026_Report.pdf__;!!DOxrgLBm!GvWpxNNoS3o2bepAZH_wm1CK821qFcTUlevYiAwCBQeeT2zfJo6y8aXbCUtXWXbk7FEwl4O3dKctNya28rzaGf7GTIYHLq_CyVNX$" target="_blank] IPC estimates indicate that cereal production in southern Somalia was 32% above the 1995–2025 long-term average), while northwestern Somalia's Gu/Karan production was 76% below the 2010–2025 average. The onset of the Deyr season rainfall has started in most parts of the country and both Copernicus and ICPAC forecasts for the remainder of the season, indicate a high likelihood of above average rainfall, linked to the ongoing El nino phenomenon and could potentially improve pasture and water availability and support livestock and crop production. However, El Niño-related heavy rainfall and flooding could adversely affect riverine and low-lying agricultural areas through crop damage, displacement and disruption of market access. Levels of acute food insecurity remain high in the country. Between October–December 2026, around 5.4 million people are in IPC Phase 3 + (Crisis or worse).

SSD.comment: Main-season harvesting is progressing under poor conditions following successive months of below-average rainfall and high temperatures. Persistent moisture deficits have affected crops and rangelands, particularly in Jonglei, Lakes, Northern Bahr el Ghazal, Unity, Warrap and Western Bahr el Ghazal. Reduced harvests and poor pasture conditions are likely to constrain household food availability and livestock productivity. Renewed conflict in Upper Nile and Jonglei, displacement, economic deterioration and arrivals from Sudan continue to compound agricultural losses and restrict access to assistance.

SWZ.comment: Planting of summer cereal crops began in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions nationwide. Furthermore, the JRC ASAP forecast warnings for both [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/ebb9f57d] crops and [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6ca9147] rangelands point to a high probability of dry conditions across agropastoral areas for the upcoming 2026–2027 season.

SYR.comment: In Syria, sowings of winter barley have started in October under very favourable rainfall conditions with twice to 5 times the average 10 mm of rainfall in the last month while wheat sowings are expected to start in November and finalize in December. Rainfall is expected to remain favourable, namely above average amount in November and then close to average through March, according to the Copernicus C3S seasonal multimodels rainfall forecast. Food insecurity remains high with about 6 million people in need of food assistance (for a total population of 24 million) according to [https://fews.net/middle-east-and-europe/syria/food-security-outlook/june-2026] FEWSNET June report, mainly as a result of the economic situation, which affects especially poor households and IDPs (despite favourable weather conditions) and reduction in humanitarian assistance in 2026.

TCD.comment: Harvesting of the 2026 coarse grains and rice crops is currently underway and is expected to conclude by December. Driven by a highly irregular rainfall distribution and high temperatures, the agricultural season is suffering from widespread moisture stress that severely impacts both the Sudanian and Sahelian zones. Nationally, more than 40% of the active crop area and close to 35% of the active rangeland area exhibit a negative greenness anomaly. Moreover, high domestic fuel prices, restricted access to fertilizer, and civil insecurity in Lac Province and the Sudanian zone are driving up agricultural costs and disrupting farming activities ([https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=TCD] FAO GIEWS (07/09)). Consequently, below-average crop and livestock production is expected.

TGO.comment: The planting of the second-season maize crop in the south was concluded in September, and crop biomass conditions as of mid-October are average to above-average thanks to near-average rainfall received over the past month. In the north, the harvesting of cereals is currently underway with generally good prospects, except for localized parts of the Savanes and Kara regions, where pockets of below-average crop biomass are observable. Additionally, the Sahel crisis spillover in the Savanes region has displaced over 68,700 individuals, including refugees, asylum seekers, and IDPs, straining local markets, natural resources, and services in host communities ([https://reliefweb.int/report/togo/wfp-togo-country-brief-october-2026] WFP Togo Country Brief, October 2026). Despite these severe humanitarian and localized climate strains, overall production remains resilient; as reported by [https://fews.net/west-africa/togo/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), "forecast cereal production for the 2026/27 season is estimated at 1,955,893 metric tons, an increase of 4.3 percent compared with 2025/26 and 25.2 percent compared with the five-year average.".

THA.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

TJK.comment: In Tajikistan, sowings of winter wheat and barley, the main crops with cotton, have started in October under seasonally low rainfall conditions and will finalize in November (in the north and center) and December (in the south). Above average rainfall is forecast for November through March according to the Copernicus C3S multimodel seasonal forecast, which is consistent with the very strong El Niño forecast till early 2027, however irrigation will remain key.

TKM.comment: In Turkmenistan, sowing of (irrigated) winter wheat is underway (till mid-November) under the usual low rainfall conditions. Above average rainfall is expected from November through March in the whole Central Asia, which should benefit to irrigation, according to the Copernicus C3S multimodel seasonal forecast, which is consistent with the recognised influence of an El Niño event.

TLS.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

TUN.comment: In Tunisia, sowings of winter cereals have just started and are expected to finalize by December. Moisture conditions have been below average with about 50% rainfall deficit in the last month; November is expected close to average but drier than average conditions should prevail from December to February according to C3S multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast.

TZA.comment: Maize is being planted in bimodal areas for the Vuli season, while planting of Msimu maize and sorghum is approaching in unimodal areas. Although most of the country is still off-season, biomass is below average in parts of the west and north, with 75% of cropland in Katavi, 81% in Kigoma and 60% in Mara showing poor vegetation status. Linked to the ongoing El Niño, [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] Copernicus seasonal forecasts point to wetter-than-usual conditions in the coming months. According to the Tanzania Meteorological Authority (TMA), conditions are already turning wetter, with rainfall on 22–23 October exceeding October monthly averages at some stations, and the heaviest rains expected between November 2026 and January 2027 ([https://thechanzo.com/2026/10/26/tma-extends-el-nino-alert-to-western-and-southern-tanzania-as-november-rains-near] The Chanzo). While this could support Vuli crop development, very strong El Niño conditions combined with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole also raise the risk of flooding, crop losses and transport disruptions ([https://www.thecitizen.co.tz/tanzania/news/national/tanzania-braces-for-heavy-rains-as-el-ni%C3%B1o-raises-flood-risks-5642818] The Citizen).

UGA.comment: First-season crops were harvested under predominantly average or favourable conditions, although localized production losses occurred. In Karamoja, below-average and poorly distributed rainfall constrained the unimodal crop, particularly in Kotido. Second-season planting is under way following a delayed and dry start in several bimodal areas. Forecast above-normal October–December rainfall could improve crop establishment and soil moisture, although flooding and waterlogging remain concerns. High food prices, localised harvest shortfalls and pressure on refugee-hosting areas continue to increase humanitarian needs. The IPC analysis covering July 2026–January 2027 estimates approximately 3.6 million people in Crisis or worse, a 6% increase compared with 2025.

UZB.comment: In Uzbekistan, sowing of winter cereals are underway till mid-November under seasonally dry conditions in the south and close to average rainfall conditions in the north. Rainfall conditions should improve in the coming months in the whole region according to the Copernicus C3S multimodel seasonal forecast, which is consistent with the recognised influence of an El Niño event.

VNM.comment: Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

YEM.comment: In Yemen, in the highlands, harvest of kharif cereals and summer wheat has started with good prospects thanks to above average biomass (in Ibb, Dhamar, Sana’A, Hajjah) while in the Coastal areas, biomass of sorghum and millet in vegetative growth is close to average, despite pockets of low biomass around Mahall Rabi’Ah and Mahwa Umm Zayn localities. In the Eastern Plateau, wheat sowings are delayed in Al Jawf, the main wheat producing governorate. Food insecurity remains high with about 18 million food insecure people out of 42 million people according to [https://www.wfp.org/countries/yemen] WFP, mainly as a result of the socio economic conditions and conflict.

ZAF.comment: The winter cereal harvest is currently underway and is expected to conclude in November. According to the [https://www.sagis.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/CEC_2026-10-27.pdf] official third production forecast, total winter wheat production is projected at 1.789 million tonnes, nearly 13% below the five-year average. Conversely, the same report estimates that 2026 barley production will be approximately 18% above the five-year average. Planting activities for summer cereal crops began in October across eastern provinces under mixed weather conditions, characterized by favourable cumulative rainfall in September followed by below-average amounts during the first two dekads of October. In western areas, planting of maize—the primary summer cereal grown—is set to start in November. Looking forward, the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions nationwide. Furthermore, the JRC ASAP forecast warnings for both [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/ebb9f57d] crops and [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6ca9147] rangelands point to a high probability of dry conditions across agropastoral areas for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. This grim outlook aligns with warnings from the [https://www.weathersa.co.za/api/wp/uploads/2026/09/SAWS-ENSO-Statement-002.pdf] South African Weather Service, which state that an exceptionally strong El Niño event has formed and is projected to bring severe below-normal rainfall, unprecedented heatwaves, and widespread water scarcity across most of South Africa during the 2026/27 summer season. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

ZMB.comment: Planting of summer cereal crops is set to begin at the end of October. However, an initial delay in the start of the season has been observed across western and northern areas, specifically affecting the Western, North-Western, Copperbelt, and Northern provinces. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of severe, drier-than-normal conditions across central and southern Zambia, contrasting with expected normal to wetter-than-average conditions in the far northern provinces. This grim outlook aligns with [https://fews.net/southern-africa/zambia/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026) reports that warn of a very strong El Niño bringing erratic, below-average rainfall and a delayed onset to southern and western Zambia, with prolonged dry spells during the critical December–February period expected to heavily constrain planting, crop growth, and agricultural labor income. Given these compounding factors, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

ZWE.comment: Planting of summer cereal crops is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_10_2-3-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for November–December 2026 indicates a high probability of drier-than-normal conditions nationwide. Furthermore, the JRC ASAP forecast warnings for both [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/ebb9f57d] crops and [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/s/f6ca9147] rangelands point to a high probability of dry conditions across agropastoral areas for the upcoming 2026–2027 season. This grim outlook aligns with reports from [https://fews.net/southern-africa/zimbabwe/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September 2026), which predict below-average rainfall and high temperatures driven by El Niño. In response, the government has approved a comprehensive six-pillar mitigation plan focused on food security, agricultural support, and financial relief ([https://farmfutureafrica.co.zw/zimbabwes-six-pillar-super-el-nino-strategy-what-farmers-need-to-know/] Farm Future Africa). Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.
